quantify

/KWAHN-tuh-fye/ - the stress falls on KWAHN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Quantify means to measure something and express it as a number or definite amount.

The insurer asked her to quantify the flood damage, so the vague 'we lost almost everything' became a nine-page inventory totaling $48,200.

Example

The sleep researchers refused to accept 'the patients seem more rested' and set out to quantify it: minutes to fall asleep, number of wakings, hours of deep sleep — until restfulness had become a column of numbers.

That conversion is the whole verb: something real but unnumbered — restedness — gets measured and expressed as figures. Quantify builds on Latin quantus, 'how much,' plus -ify, 'to make': literally, to make into a how-much.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

measure: Measure means to find a thing's size or extent against a standard; quantify goes one step further — the result must come out as an explicit number, not just 'longer' or 'warmer.'

calculate: Calculate means to work a number out from other numbers by arithmetic; quantifying starts earlier, turning something unnumbered — fear, fog, loyalty — into figures a calculation could then use.

gauge: Gauge means to estimate an amount, often roughly and by instinct; you can gauge a crowd's mood in a glance, but to quantify it you would need a count.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

guess: to judge without evidence or a count

intuit: to sense something without measuring it

Where it sits · how exactly the amount gets pinned down

gauge → quantify → enumerate

gauge vs. quantify: Gauge is looser than quantify: gauging settles for a feel — 'about thirty, maybe' — while quantifying isn't finished until an actual number is on the page.

enumerate vs. quantify: Enumerate goes past quantify: quantifying settles on a total, while enumerating counts the items off one by one until every single member is listed.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — quant-: how much (Latin quantus)

Suffix — -ify: to make (Latin facere)

Put it together: Latin quantus asked 'how much?' and -ify (from facere, 'to make') turns the question into a verb: to make something into a how-much. The root kept its shape in English — quantity is its plainest child — and the family still does the counting wherever counting is done.

Use the root in a new word: quantum: Long after fault was settled, the tribunal was still arguing over the quantum of damages.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Quantify is the verb of skeptics and scientists: it demands that a claim trade its adjectives for figures. It shines with things that resist numbers — morale, risk, pain — and sounds redundant with things already numbered; nobody needs to quantify a price tag. 'Hard to quantify' is the phrase's natural habitat.
